passage:
Sudha's hardware shop in the market town had a new problem. Farmers could not leave their fields at harvest, and kept asking for pipes and hinges to be brought out to them. Nobody knew how to do it.
On Saturday evening after closing, Sudha, Farida and the two helpers sat on the shop floor with a roll of paper. "Say any idea, even silly ones," said Sudha. A boy on a cycle. A phone list of orders. A weekly round to the farms with the pickup. Someone joked about a drone.
The paper filled up and nobody said no. When the tea was cold they had eighteen ideas, and they circled three that would cost little to try. "Nobody here has done this before," said Farida, "so we'll have to invent it."

qa.q: How many ideas did the team have at the end?
What did Sudha want from the team by saying even silly ideas were welcome?
qa.a: Sudha wanted everyone to feel free and hopeful about sharing, because there was no known answer to copy.

qa.q: What could the team do after circling three ideas?
qa.a: They could try the cheapest idea on a small scale and see how farmers react, since only real use shows what works.

qa.q: How might the farmers see the new plan?
qa.a: Farmers who cannot leave their fields at harvest may welcome pipes and hinges being brought out to them.

grounding: A team facing a new customer problem gathers many ideas before choosing, since there is no precedent to copy.

passage: At the small bike-repair company in Lisbon, a new problem had come up: food delivery riders were bringing electric bikes with battery issues nobody on the team had seen before. Diego, the manager, gathered the five mechanics around the workbench on Monday morning. "We don't have a manual for this. Nobody's done it before us. So let's not pick the first idea. Let's get many." Zeynep wrote on the whiteboard as ideas came: partner with a battery specialist, train one mechanic, a weekend repair clinic for riders, a quick-check service, even a loan-bike scheme. Twelve ideas in twenty minutes. Some were silly. Then they circled three to try. Diego looked at the board. "None of us would have thought of all this alone."

qa.q: How many ideas did the team come up with?
How did Diego feel looking at the board?
qa.a: Diego felt pleased and a little amazed, seeing the group had found far more than anyone alone.

qa.q: Why did brainstorming suit this problem?
qa.a: It was new with no manual or past example to copy, so many different ideas gave better options to choose from.

qa.q: How might Zeynep have felt writing the ideas?
qa.a: Zeynep was probably energised and amused, especially by the silly ideas mixed in with good ones.

grounding: A team facing a new customer problem gathers many ideas before choosing, since there is no precedent and diverse thinking helps.

passage: In the meeting room of the telemedicine start-up, Zubin put one question on the screen: "Elderly patients in small towns miss video appointments. Why, and what can we do?" No one had solved this before; the company was two years old. Aadhya, from customer support, said, "Should we just copy what city hospitals do?" Zubin shook his head. "City patients are different. We need lots of ideas first, then pick." For twenty-five minutes, everyone threw ideas on sticky notes: phone-call option, a helper at the local pharmacy, reminder calls in the local language, larger buttons, appointments at the village health centre. Aadhya added three herself. By the end there were thirty notes on the wall. They grouped them and chose two to test first.

qa.q: How many notes were on the wall by the end?
How might Aadhya have felt adding three ideas herself?
qa.a: She probably felt more confident and included, moving from suggesting copying to offering her own ideas.

qa.q: Why was brainstorming a better fit than copying city hospitals?
qa.a: The problem was new for this group of patients, so gathering many different ideas gave options a copy would miss.

qa.q: How might the elderly patients be affected by this approach?
qa.a: They might get solutions that fit their lives, like phone calls or help at the pharmacy, instead of ones made for city patients.

grounding: A team facing a new customer problem gathers many ideas before choosing, since there is no precedent to copy.
